#4852. Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

Plus, the difference between the two resistance training methods.

When it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body. And it's true: Maintaining muscle mass is essential for staying healthy, mobile, and independent as you get older. But here's something you might not realize: Having more muscle doesn't necessarily mean you're stronger. And when it comes to living as long (and as well!) as possible, that distinction matters.

Resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength. Training for muscle growth, known as hypertrophy training, focuses on increasing the size of your muscles, says Vonda Wright, MD, an orthopedic surgeon who researches longevity and muscle health.

On the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce. It’s often measured by how much weight you can lift in a particular exercise, Dr. Wright explains. Although larger muscles have the potential to produce more force, muscle size alone doesn’t determine strength. “That’s why someone who is smaller can sometimes be stronger than someone with visibly larger muscles,” she adds.

Meet the experts: Vonda Wright, MD, is an orthopedic surgeon and author of Unbreakable. Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute in Atlanta. Stuart Phillips, PhD, is a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Ben Walker, CPT, is a personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland.

Still, both adaptations play an important role in healthy aging—especially since muscle mass and strength naturally decline with age. Building muscle supports your joints and bones, helps regulate metabolic health, and gives you the strength and physical capacity to keep moving and stay active, says Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute. Strength, meanwhile, allows you to put that muscle to work, whether you’re carrying groceries, climbing stairs, or getting up from the floor, he explains.

It’s imperative to build both strength and muscle for a long, healthy life. But if your goal is to stay active and independent well into your later years, one may be worth prioritizing over the other.

Resistance training can help you build muscle and become stronger, but these are distinct goals that emphasize different outcomes. Training for muscle growth focuses on increasing muscle size, while training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force you can produce, says Kovacs. The two goals overlap, and people typically gain both muscle and strength through resistance training. But you can formulate your workouts to emphasize one outcome over the other, he adds.

For instance, if your goal is maximal strength, the weight you lift matters more. So, training for strength means practicing movements with loads that feel heavy to you, says Stuart Phillips, PhD, a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Strength gains depend not only on muscle size, but also on how effectively your nervous system activates your muscles and how efficiently you perform the movement. “Lighter weights can still make you stronger, but taking them to failure doesn’t automatically make them equivalent to heavier training for maximizing strength,” Phillips explains. For this goal, he recommends 2 to 3 sets of roughly 4 to 8 reps with a challenging weight, stopping before your technique breaks down.

In terms of muscle growth, both lighter and heavier weights can build muscle—what matters is that your body is sufficiently challenged. Of course, lighter weights will require more repetitions to grow muscle, Phillips says. (In fact, his research shows that performing roughly 20 to 25 repetitions with light weights produced similar muscle growth to sets of 8 to 12 repetitions with heavier weights when both were taken to failure.)

As a rule of thumb, Phillips recommends choosing a weight that makes the last few reps feel challenging while leaving about two good reps in reserve. (If you finish 25 reps and feel like you could easily do five more, the weight is probably too light to provide enough of a stimulus to spark growth.) One way to gauge this is with the resistance-training rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scale, which measures how hard a set feels based on how many more reps you think you could complete with good form, he explains. The scale runs from 1 to 10: An RPE of eight means you could squeeze out about two more reps, a 9 means you have one left, and a 10 means you’ve reached failure and can’t complete another rep.

The number of sets you perform matters for building muscle, too. Doing one challenging set per exercise consistently over time can grow muscle, Phillips says, but research suggests that performing multiple sets generally leads to greater muscle growth.

Strength, which is the maximum force you can produce in a particular task, directly influences how well you can move through everyday life. “Strong muscles support our skeleton, protect our joints, improve metabolic health, and allow us to continue doing the things we love at 50, 70, and 90,” says Dr. Wright. Strength helps us with getting up off the floor, carrying our own suitcase, climbing a mountain, playing with grandchildren, and living independently long-term.

Consider something as simple as getting out of a chair. When you’re younger and stronger, Kovacs says that movement may require only a small percentage of your maximum strength. As you lose strength with age, though, that same movement requires more of what you have available. If you aren’t regularly training it, everyday activities can become increasingly difficult, he explains. But when you continue to build strength as you age, you have more to pull from, making those activities easier.

Additionally, research draws a direct connection between strength and a longer life: A 2026 study in JAMA Network Open looked at the association between muscular strength and mortality. Over 5,000 women ages 63 to 99 underwent testing for grip strength, chair stand performance, and a timed walk test. Participants also mailed health update questionnaires annually between 2012 and 2014 until 2023. They found that higher muscle strength was associated with lower mortality.

Strength training is also associated with cardiometabolic benefits, endurance performance, and bone density—which are all important for living long and well. In fact, a small 2022 study in Sensors had 29 postmenopausal women with osteopenia or osteoporosis (when you have lower bone mineral density than normal) either do strength training exercises with heavy and moderately heavy weights, or no exercise at all, for six months. The group that strength trained had higher bone mineral density at the end of the trial period.

Muscle is one of your body’s best forms of insurance for getting older. Everyday activities depend on having enough muscle (as well as strength) to do them independently. “Muscle supports our joints and loads our bones, helping stimulate the bone-building process, but it’s also essential to mobility and functional strength," Dr. Wright explains. “If we want to continue getting ourselves off the ground, climbing stairs, carrying things, traveling, playing sports, and living independently, we need muscle to do it.”

Research also concludes that less muscle mass is associated with a higher risk of mortality. A 2023 review in PLOS One observed 16 studies with over 81,000 participants and looked at the connection between their body composition and when they died. The review concluded that a low skeletal muscle mass index was significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality.

Additionally, having muscle mass can improve your metabolic health. A 2025 study in Nutrition & Metabolism had older participants with type 2 diabetes either build muscle through resistance training alone, resistance training and eating a whey protein supplement, or doing neither of the two, for 12 weeks. Those who completed the muscle-building interventions significantly improved their blood glucose control and insulin resistance.

Plus, lower muscle mass is linked to poor balance and a higher risk of falls. So, maintaining muscle helps protect your mobility and independence as you age, Dr. Wright adds. A 2020 study in Menopause Review had 122 women over 60 do physical performance tests (gait speed test, grip strength, and a timed up and go). Their body composition was measured, and they filled out a survey of how often they fell in the past year. Less muscle was associated with a higher risk of falls.

A well-rounded workout plan should naturally progress both muscular size and strength. After all, they address different pieces of the same puzzle and one form of training can help you make progress in the other. As you build muscle, you generally increase the amount of tissue available to produce force, says Ben Walker, CPT, a certified personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland. And as you train for strength, your brain and nervous system become better at coordinating and activating those muscles, he explains.

If you’re looking for a plan that’ll help you build both strength and muscle, check out our Women’s Health+ exclusive workout plans. Each one comes with four weeks of expert-programmed workouts, science-backed nutrition advice, and evidence-based recovery methods.

Remember, longevity isn’t about simply adding years to your life. It’s about extending your healthspan, or the number of years you remain healthy, mobile, and strong. “The goal is to bring our healthspan as close to our lifespan as possible, and for me, that means building a body that can carry you through the life you want to live,” says Dr. Wright. That way, you’ll be ready to throw grandkids around at 60, deadlift hundreds of pounds at 70, and lift your own suitcase on vacation with your family in your 80s and beyond.

#4851. Is Yeti’s New Performance Outdoor Clothing Any Good? I Put It to the Test to Find Out.

Sizing up the new apparel drop from the cooler and drinkware giant.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently launched a performance outdoor clothing line. It’s a deviation, sure, but perhaps a sensible one given the brand’s commitment to outdoor gear and all things insulation. As frequent testers of new products in this ever-expanding category, we could not resist the chance to throw them on and put them through the paces in the elements.

We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip. For context, the other two pieces are the Caprock Merino Quarter-Zip and the Heuco 310 Full-Zip, essentially siblings of the fleece we tried out. To the brand’s credit, no PFAs are used in the line and all items come with a three-year warranty.

Before even testing, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. The pieces show some clear restraint from a brand that tends toward boldness and large logos (you know, like the beloved coolers). You’d barely even know these were Yeti tops, as you really have to hunt for the brand stamp. And there’s a less-is-more approach in the design here, clearly made with active lifestyles and packability in mind (even color-wise, there are only two options max per item, a somewhat refreshing factoid).

I tried all three pieces over a couple of weeks in the dead of fall in the Pacific Northwest. Translation? They were subjected to downpours, foggy night jogs, chilly mornings, and windy afternoons. I wore them on long walks with the dog, bike commutes in the rain, adventures on muddy trails, and to evening soccer games. I even brought them to the coast during a storm that stirred up high surf and sideways precipitation. Here’s what I think after all the initial testing.

The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket looks good, there’s no denying as much. The sleek, trim fit works for even the most active functions and we found it never overheated in testing. Lightweight and packable, it’s somewhat nimble thanks to two-way stretch fabric but not as much so as the other two items tested.

The water resistance is also impressive. I walked the dog through a downpour in this jacket for about 30 minutes and came back with just a few moisture spots on my layer beneath. Not bad for a jacket that certainly doesn’t claim to be waterproof (though does sport a water-repellant finish). In drizzle and light rain, you’re just fine in this puffer jacket. In fact, the water would bead up with the same intensity even after many wears, meaning that exterior was done right.

While I liked the felt-lined pockets, I think they could be even warmer. The blend of Expedry Down and traceable European Lavalan Wool insulation is perhaps the jacket’s strongest feature. Going with a hybrid blend affords an ability to tightrope walk that fine-line between breathability and protection from the elements—and the proof was in the performance.

At $400 though, this is not a cheap item by any stretch of the imagination.

This was my favorite piece of the trio, and arguably the most straightforward. From the superior YKK Aquaguard zipper to the extremely packable nature of the jacket, the Tilloo is a genuine winner. Like a big boss in your favorite video game, so many jackets in the category have a weak spot hidden somewhere. It usually translates to water seeping in from a cuff or finding its way in through an average zipper. Not here—this jacket is watertight yet breathable.

One of the coolest features is just how quiet this jacket is. As somebody born and raised in the Pacific Northwest, I’ve worn a fair number of waterproof shells. Many of them swish loudly as you move (not unlike Jim Carrey in Dumb and Dumber as he’s pretending to run while driving). This less crinkly option is quite quiet, a bonus you perhaps never knew you desired (but once you have it, it’s hard to go back).

If you’re like me, you like to get outdoors to get away from all the noise. A loud jacket can disrupt an adventure, whether you’re birding in a marsh or scanning for wildlife on a hike. This jacket is not silent but it’s noticeably more hushed than most others, even during animated motions and heavy exercise. The Velcro cuffs create nice clasps over base layers (or just above a smartwatch during a run) while the liner itself is fairly soft to the touch, unlike the less appealing, membrane-like feel you get from so many options. The hood is adjustable and offers a nice panorama without hampering much of your view. And the way it pulls rain off is impressive, meaning you never have to shake off pooling areas like you might with a lesser jacket or umbrella.

It has become my go-to for offseason excursions. While $350 is an undeniable expense, the jacket is worth the price.

Straight on, the Sansaba Fleece 260 is incredibly soft (like, you’re gonna want to nuzzle it). The proprietary PrimaLoft Bio Fleece is a sensory joy, with a lovely feel and a density level that seems to hit the Goldilocks spot. Best, it’s a composite of 100% post-consumer recycled materials. These shorter fibers are densely distributed, creating what Yeti classifies as a midweight garment. We’d argue that it performs on the higher end of the spectrum, at least in terms of insulation and warmth. No, it wouldn’t quite cut it on its own for significant stretches in below-freezing conditions, but it does just find in the kind of cold we’re normally subjected to.

The fleece also breathes quite well. I found that it paired nicely with a brisk mountain hike or even a sweaty workout in damp conditions. However, playing under anything more than a light drizzle requires a proper shell to fend off precipitation. We liked the length of the collar, stylish yet still big enough to hide under during chilly gusts of wind.

Billed as a fleece made for movement and strenuous activities, the Sansaba fared pretty well. I really put it to the sword one day, zipping it up for a four-mile run in light rain. Normally, I’d wear a long-sleeve moisture-wicking shirt beneath, but I wanted to see how the fleece would fare atop a regular cotton T-shirt. While it did well at fending off light moisture and pulling some of the sweat from my arms, I was pretty soaked in sweat at the end. A pretty easy fix with a better undershirt, sure, but it indicates that perhaps the fleece can’t quite do the most strenuous activities without an unwanted side effect (props for drying so quickly after the fact, however).

Additional cons? The interior of the pockets could use some work. The plain mesh is boring and doesn’t do much to warm the paws. But the fleece is so warm and welcoming throughout the top that you can just rest your hands elsewhere for a quick warm-up. The collar also hugs the neck nicely. This is bittersweet, as it really cradles the area and keeps it warm; however, if you like to duck your chin and mouth (and a little nose) beneath this part of a top during a wind gust, it’s harder to do as it’s fairly snug. For $180, this is a pretty good deal, but not necessarily superior to several other fleeces at a similar price point.

While you don’t need the whole set, you might want a few of these pieces to bolster your outdoor apparel game. I recommend them all, but with some caveats. The rain jacket is the best item for the price and is very much on par with others in the category.

The puffer is nice but I don’t find it a whole lot better than, say, this one from Wren that I’ve been wearing for a couple of years now (the Columbia Terwilliger Treail Heat Seal Jacket is another fine option). The neat, textured, and non-glossy (per so, so many) look is hard to beat, but it’s a significant chunk of change even give its merits.

The fleece is also an attractive piece of outerwear with some high-performance capabilities, but perhaps not at the same level as some of its counterparts at its decidedly high price point. I tends toward options like the Patagonia Better Jacket and the Trailmade from REI, a bargain-and-a-half. But the Sansaba is an undoubtedly good-looking option with a lot going for it.

Yeti is clearly on to something here and has turned heads with a combination of clean fits, useful tech, and designs with mobility in mind (not to mention some environmentally conscious moves too). But this writer would suggest splurging on perhaps just one of the items depending on your adventuring angles and lifestyle.

#4850. Europol follows $28.5M crypto trail in streaming piracy crackdown

Authorities from 11 countries worked with Binance, Coinbase and Chainalysis to trace financial transactions and disrupt illegal streaming services.

Law enforcement authorities from 11 countries, working with crypto exchanges Binance and Coinbase and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, have traced more than 26 million euros ($28.5 million) in cryptocurrency transactions and disrupted 57 illegal streaming services in an operation coordinated by Europol, the law enforcement agency of the European Union.

In a Tuesday announcement, Europol said the five-day operation took place in Seville, Spain, from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 and identified 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, attracting more than 7.3 million annual visits combined.

Europol said illegal streaming operators often collect subscription payments in cryptocurrency, allowing them to transfer funds quickly across borders. Investigators traced blockchain transactions to identify links between streaming services, cryptocurrency wallets and the individuals controlling them.

The EU’s law enforcement agency said the operation reflects a shift from focusing solely on shutting down illegal streaming services to also targeting the financial infrastructure behind them. The findings will support ongoing national investigations, including efforts to identify suspects and trace assets linked to criminal activity.

According to figures from the Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance cited by Europol, an estimated 60 million people across Europe use unauthorized internet protocol television (IPTV) services, with estimated annual losses of 4.83 billion euros ($5.3 billion) for legitimate providers and a further 1.08 billion euros ($1.18 billion) in unpaid taxes for governments.

Related: Tron and Tether bring in Chainalysis after T3 crime unit folds

The operation follows other international efforts to disrupt criminal networks and their financial infrastructure. In March, US and European authorities dismantled SocksEscort, a malicious proxy service that enabled crimes including bank fraud and cryptocurrency account takeovers.

The service allowed customers to pay anonymously in cryptocurrency and received at least $5.7 million in user payments, according to investigators. Authorities froze about $3.5 million in cryptocurrency linked to the operation.

Earlier that month, Europol and the FBI took down LeakBase, a cybercrime forum with more than 142,000 registered users. An earlier cybercrime marketplace, RaidForums, had previously hosted leaked personal data belonging to users of crypto hardware wallet provider Ledger.

#4849. BYD’s full-size luxury SUV has a wheel problem, and it’s fixing it for free

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

After opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a new record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD said the issue stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

The company said it “immediately” launched an investigation and corrected the issue so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit issues like this going forward.

BYD said the issue does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

The company said owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD said, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

In comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

Based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li said the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

#4848. Anthropic’s Claude Ship Lets AI Write, Review and Approve Its Own Code

Anthropic’s Claude Ship Lets AI Write, Review and Approve Its Own Code

Anthropic is automating another part of software engineering: the process of deciding whether the code an AI writes is actually good enough to use.

The company introduced Claude Ship on Monday, a collection of AI agents capable of reviewing software changes, fixing errors, and approving code according to rules established by development teams.

Under certain configurations, software changes can make their way into a company's codebase without a human reading a single line of code.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

AI coding tools have become so good at producing software that reviewing it has become a bottleneck. Developers who previously spent hours writing a feature can now generate several in that time, but someone still has to check whether those changes work without breaking something else.

Anthropic is experiencing that problem itself. The company says Claude already writes most of the code produced by its Claude Code team.

Claude Ship combines three tools, each responsible for a different stage of the process. The first, Code Review, examines proposed changes against the existing codebase, using multiple agents to find potential bugs and verify each other's findings.

PR Steward, the second tool, makes the necessary corrections when automated tests fail or reviewers identify problems. It documents its modifications and provides instructions for reversing them, allowing developers to intervene if necessary.

The third tool, Claude Approvals, decides whether the proposed changes satisfy the company's approval policies. According to Anthropic's technical documentation, repositories configured for automatic merging can incorporate changes without anyone manually approving them.

The ability to delegate code reviews to AI is particularly attractive in the age of vibe coding, where developers—and increasingly people with little programming experience—build software by describing what they want in natural language.

But having an AI double-check another AI's work doesn't necessarily eliminate their shared weaknesses. A human programmer and a language model might approach a problem differently, whereas two agents powered by similar models could overlook the same flawed assumption.

A peer-reviewed study published earlier this year found that models from OpenAI and Anthropic performed slightly better at identifying and repairing security vulnerabilities in human-written code than in AI-generated code.

AI-assisted software development has already produced some expensive mistakes. In April, a startup founder reported that a coding agent running Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 deleted his company's production database and its volume-level backups through a single API call.

Anthropic's own experience with automated code reviews illustrates a different problem: AI agents can get stuck correcting each other. In one instance, according to an October engineering report, a proposed software change went through more than 50 rounds of automated reviews and corrections overnight before its author intervened.

The company nevertheless reported encouraging internal results. The number of merged changes more than doubled between June and September, while the proportion of changes that had to be reversed fell by more than 40%.

Those results came from a broader review process that retained human oversight for sensitive modifications, rather than a fully autonomous system. Changes to documentation can pass without human approval at Anthropic, whereas particularly risky modifications require two people to sign off.

“A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it,” Anthropic's engineers wrote.

Whether other companies adopt equally restrictive policies is up to them. Claude Ship allows administrators to determine which parts of their software require human supervision and which decisions they are comfortable delegating to an AI.

The service is available for GitHub repositories on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, with charges based on token consumption. For now, Anthropic recommends running its automated approval system in observation mode, letting the AI demonstrate what it would have approved before giving it the authority to do so.

#4847. Hackers breach CIA intelligence network in latest US cyberattack

The reported breach follows cyber incidents involving the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and Department of Agriculture.

The US Central Intelligence Agency and at least one other intelligence agency have been hit with a cybersecurity breach that exposed unclassified information, according to The New York Times.

Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Times reported that hackers breached a network used by the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence that analyzes publicly available information to gather intelligence insights.

It is also believed that other government agencies were exposed in the breach, according to two of the people.

An official with the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems. Cointelegraph reached out to the CIA for comment.

The breach adds to a spate of reported cyber incidents at US federal agencies in recent weeks.

The Verge on Tuesday reported the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is also investigating a “cybersecurity incident” that “resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It is not clear if it is related to the recent CIA breach.

Other breaches include the US Department of Agriculture, a leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel records and a hack of the FBI’s national crime database.

Speaking to ABC News about the FBI attack on Sunday, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said cyberattacks have been increasing, and digital infrastructure needs to be upgraded.

“In 2020, there were roughly 750,000 cyber incidents reported to the FBI. That’s now up to over a million cyber incidents,” said Clayton.

“And what we’re seeing, though, here, and I want the American people to know this, is we have a step change in technology that we’re facing with superintelligence and computing power that is expanding exponentially and we have a dated digital infrastructure.”

Clayton declined to discuss the specifics of the FBI incident but said that cyber incidents were not a new phenomenon.

“Cyber probing, cyber incidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time.”

#4844. CleanSpark weighs selling more Bitcoin than it mines to de-risk books

The Bitcoin miner sold 2,102 BTC while it produced just 1,708 BTC in the September quarter.

Bitcoin miner CleanSpark is considering selling more Bitcoin than it mines each quarter to reduce its treasury risk, according to chief financial officer Gary Vecchiarelli, potentially further drawing down its holdings, last valued at $806 million.

CleanSpark held 13,530 Bitcoin at the end of September after mining 1,708 Bitcoin and selling 2,102 Bitcoin during the quarter, according to Cointelegraph’s tally of the company’s monthly operating updates. It marks the first time since at least 2024 that the company ended the quarter with less Bitcoin than it began with.

During a Q4 earnings call on Tuesday, Vecchiarelli said CleanSpark already aims to sell virtually all of the Bitcoin it mines to cover day-to-day operating costs, and told an analyst that selling slightly more than it produces in a quarter was one way to reduce treasury risk.

“We see the selling of a small amount of Bitcoin in excess of the quarterly production to be one way of de-risking,” said Vecchiarelli.

“But again, we are going to be sensitive and very reactionary to markets, and we are going to use that capital to make sure that we prevent dilution or bringing additional debt just to grow the company,” he said.

The remarks came as CleanSpark recorded a $987 million net loss for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, compared with a net income of $364 million a year earlier. The company attributed two-thirds of the swing to noncash adjustments in the value of its Bitcoin holdings, as Bitcoin’s price fell from about $114,100 to $83,600 over the fiscal year.

Related: Trump-linked American Bitcoin secures $150M credit line from FalconX

CleanSpark also said it sold an undisclosed amount of Bitcoin since September to raise cash for expected acquisitions, as Vecchiarelli said it continues to view its Bitcoin holdings as “a liquid source of non-dilutive capital.”

CleanSpark also cut about 25,000 machines from its Bitcoin mining fleet in the September quarter, bringing the number in operation to about 200,000.

Vecchiarelli said the reduction improved energy efficiency to 14.8 joules per terahash from 15.8 in the previous quarter, which he said should help CleanSpark stay profitable if mining conditions deteriorate ahead of the 2028 Bitcoin halving.

“Going forward, in terms of hash rate, that will probably fluctuate, but we will continue to mine so as long as it’s profitable.”

In Sandersville, Georgia, CleanSpark said its first AI data hall remains on track for the fourth quarter of 2027. CleanSpark said it expects to start unplugging miners at the site in late 2027 as the data center comes online, then decide whether to relocate or sell them.

CleanSpark shares dropped 7.5% on Tuesday ahead of the earnings release to $5.12 and are down 2.25% in after-hours trading.

The company recorded $576.5 million in total revenue in the full year, down 25% from the previous fiscal year. Adjusted EBITDA came in at a loss of $304.2 million for the year.

#4843. OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release

OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release

Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly concerned that their companies' most advanced AI models may never be safe enough for public release, according to a Tuesday report by Axios citing more than two dozen sources familiar with internal discussions.

Some researchers believe the technical problems can eventually be solved. Others reportedly want the companies to stop training more intelligent models altogether.

The report comes two days after Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned that humanity might be approaching a point where it can no longer effectively supervise artificial intelligence. Wang argued that decisions made over the next year could determine whether humans retain control over increasingly autonomous, self-improving AI systems.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

His warning followed Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's announcement that an unreleased version of Claude had helped him prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had frustrated researchers for 167 years.

The same intellectual abilities that make these models so valuable for scientific research are making them harder to supervise. A model capable of spotting something that generations of mathematicians missed could conceivably spot weaknesses in a safety system that its developers overlooked.

One of the biggest problems facing AI researchers involves reinforcement learning, a training technique that rewards models for successfully completing tasks. It's largely responsible for the impressive reasoning abilities of modern AI systems, but it can also teach them to cheat.

Researchers call this reward hacking. A model might, for example, manipulate the software responsible for grading its work instead of actually solving the problem it was assigned.

Anthropic encountered a version of this problem in February, when researchers reversed three days of training on Claude Mythos Preview after discovering undesirable behaviors. An internal review later flagged more than 10% of its active training environments for problems that included opportunities for cheating and incorrectly configured tasks.

Another problem involves chain-of-thought monitoring, which allows researchers to inspect the intermediate reasoning an AI generates before producing an answer or taking an action. Some unreleased models are increasingly capable of obscuring that reasoning or generating misleading explanations that satisfy their monitors.

In other words, the explanation researchers receive may no longer accurately reflect how the model arrived at its decision.

OpenAI has already experienced the real-world consequences of inadequate containment. The company acknowledged that an internal research model was primarily responsible for compromising AI development platform Hugging Face while pursuing a difficult task.

Keeping the smartest models away from ChatGPT and Claude users would therefore address only part of the problem.

“Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios.

OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed Sunday that AI developers agree on common limits to model development, based partly on perplexity—a mathematical measure of how accurately a model predicts subsequent pieces of text, with lower scores indicating better predictions.

Pachocki argues that companies should agree not to cross certain thresholds until researchers develop more effective ways of monitoring AI behavior. He estimates that AI-assisted research could substantially accelerate the development of new models as early as 2027.

Getting competing companies to voluntarily slow down could prove particularly difficult, especially as investors expect returns on the enormous amounts of money pouring into AI infrastructure. Anthropic itself raised more than $81 billion when it went public last week.

OpenAI said last week that it would suspend training or withhold models again if they failed to satisfy its safety requirements. Anthropic has separately committed to publishing a policy proposal on independent AI evaluators by December 15, followed by a framework addressing the pace of AI development by January 15, 2027.

#4842. These Fragrances Double As Skincare Products

We’re often told that certain scent ingredients can cause sensitivity and irritation. The latest innovations aim to do the exact opposite, nurturing your outer layer with next-generation formulas.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always had an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures a mood, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

Dual-purpose beauty products used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two issues at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” says Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver,” Do continues.

Meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

As skincare and scent merges into a brand-new category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” says Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so you can reap the benefits.

Skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent of skin in order to complement it rather than overpower it,” says Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies.

It’s all comes down to body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

But it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another layer on top of that existing baseline, Do says.

Unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”

Dr. Queller says that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “A higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation,” she says. “However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”

Deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “You can’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle scents can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she says the skin barrier may already be impaired.

So, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she says it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

The latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, says Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence important cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study showed that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

It’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The new Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

Future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-new blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist

Salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum

Each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

So, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”

What is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this new fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”

#4841. Trump willing to pardon Jensen Huang, says it won’t be necessary

The president’s remarks come days before Jensen Huang is due to face congressional questioning over national security concerns and US chip export controls.

US President Donald Trump has left the door open to pardoning Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, though he said he doesn’t think it’ll be necessary.

Trump made the comments during an interview with the New York Post just a day after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO amid scrutiny over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and whether he allowed the company’s chips to fall into China’s hands.

Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes, Trump told The Post: “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”

Trump had earlier claimed credit for pushing Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back — a move which saw Nvidia’s stock surge on Monday.

Huang is scheduled to testify before lawmakers in a closed-door, transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1.

On Dec. 3, Huang is set to be the sole witness in a hearing by the Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs about US export controls.

#4840. The 15 Best Jeans for Men, Tested and Reviewed by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FEW MENSWEAR PIECES nail durability and easy style in one package like a great pair of jeans. For me, it’s the starting point for most of my outfits. But once you start paying attention, you realize how wide the gap is between pairs that just look good and pairs that can go with a bunch of different looks. Some are so stiff like a straitjacket, others stretch out so much they feel like leggings rather than denim.

Over the past five years, I’ve tested more than 60 pairs across seasons—winter layering, dead-of-summer heat, and everything in between—alongside Men’s Health’s fashion team. We looked at different fits, washes, and cuts across a range of builds and style preferences. Skinny fits are out. Instead, go for relaxed, straight, or straight-slim cuts that fall at the widest part of your legs for a flattering drape.

The Levi’s 501 is the blueprint of jeans—the one that every other pair takes notes from. I’ve had the straight-leg style in my closet for some years now and it fits comfortably every time. It has an easy fit through the hip and thigh, with a slight taper below the knee that doesn’t stack over my shoes. The 501s is made with 100% cotton, that’s sturdy and substantial but still breathable, even in the subway where things feel stuffy.

Levi’s offers five different inseams, which is not standard for most retail denim brands. There’s also plenty of washes and different levels of stretch including low and high stretch as well none at all. In other words, whether you’re tall, short, or somewhere in between, there’s an option for everyone and you can skip wasting money at a tailor. I found that the low-stretch pair gives you enough flex to move around without any stiffness. The no-stretch version broke in nicely after a few wears, and the high-stretch ones felt more laid-back without losing shape, but just a tad less breathable.

I’ve washed the 501s a million times and the fit always held up. It hasn’t become too baggy or too tight. Though I’ve machine dried mine before and only saw minimal shrinkage, I still recommend air drying to keep the fit where it’s at. The button fly took a minute to get used to, but it adds to that vintage feel. Out of all the washes I tried, the medium stonewash was the standout. It’s soft straight out of the box, with just the right amount of fading. It works with everything in my closet: t-shirts and hoodies, oxford shirts and loafers, boots and sneakers.

This pair of travel jeans from Bonobos is the most flexible jean I’ve tested. Honestly, they wear more like athletic pants than traditional denim. The brand uses a stretch cotton blend with a generous dose of elastane, which gives you full range of motion to handle all kinds of airport chaos: twisting and turning through TSA, sprinting to your gate, or squeezing into a tight middle seat.

I usually fly in sweatpants because I can’t stand feeling restricted on long flights, but these jeans completely changed that. On a 13-hour flight back from Japan, I stayed comfortable the entire time. No pinching, no stiffness, and I wasn’t overheating, either. The fabric is super breathable and lightweight, so even during hot layovers and road trips, I didn’t feel like I was melting.

Another big win: they hold their shape. A lot of high-stretch jeans get that saggy, baggy-knee look after a few hours, but not these. I’ve worn and washed them multiple times, and they still bounce back. And despite the gym-pant-level flexibility, they still look like real jeans; clean, tailored, and polished.

They’re also extremely low-maintenance. I packed them tightly into a carry-on for hours, pulled them out, and didn’t see a single crease. That wrinkle resistance is impressive. They looked crisp and ready to wear, no steamer or iron needed. And in true Bonobos fashion: they come in more waist sizes and fits than just about any brand we’ve tested, so no matter your build, you’ll find a version that works for you.

Abercrombie has one of the strongest takes on the baggy jeans right now. This style of denim in general has fully made its comeback, showing up on runways all the way down to everyday streetwear. The brand’s offering is easy to wear: lightweight, super relaxed through the leg, and has that slight “puddle” at the shoe—meaning the hem stacks a bit over your sneakers instead of hitting right at the ankle.

I like that it comes in multiple inseams, so you can actually control how much stacking you want depending on your height or how you like your jeans to sit. And with 20-plus colorways, it’s easy to find a version that fits your vibe, whether you want something low-key and neutral or a little more standout. I personally love the vintage black wash that reads clean and modern, even with the looser shape. In terms of fabric, it’s made from 100% cotton that already feels broken-in, so you’re not dealing with anything overly structured out of the gate.

I put on the Ford Standard Jean from Buck Mason, and could instantly feel how durable this pair was. Not only is this denim as tough as they come, it’s built to last and looks damn good doing it. It’s sourced from Japan’s Kaihara mills, which is known for blending traditional shuttle loom techniques with modern innovation. In other words, this fabric has that rich, textured character you expect from premium Japanese denim, but with a level of consistency that ensures long-term durability. At 14 oz, these jeans sit in that sweet spot—not too heavy, not too light—so it feels sturdy but won’t take forever to break in.

Unlike classic 100% cotton, this pair has a hint of stretch that lets me move freely from the jump. The mid-rise sits perfectly at my waist and I noticed the cut is straight through the thighs, giving ample room to breathe and take big, confident strides. If you’ve got some serious quads, that’s not a problem. These jeans can handle your muscles without compromising your style. It tapers neatly down below the knee, laying right on your sneakers for a clean, sharp finish. Whether I’m keeping it casual with a tee or dressing it up with a crisp button-down and blazer, it has that versatile edge to switch things up.

Most selvedge denim is super stiff like cardboard, but that’s not the case with this pair from 3sixteen. Since the cotton fabric blend is infused with a hint of spandex, it's wearable out of the gate. I didn’t go through an annoying break-in period, so I could actually sit down, bike to the bodega, or bend down low without cutting off circulation. The straight fit gives me breathing room instead of feeling painted on. It’s tapered in all the right places so you get that clean, tailored silhouette without feeling like you borrowed your little cousin’s pants. And they’re not stacking weird at the ankle or drowning your sneakers; these sit just right, especially cuffed.

This is Japanese selvedge denim from Kuroki Mills: a denim mill famed for its high-quality fabrics and innovative production techniques like indigo dyeing. Yes, the pair is priced north of $300, but you get your cost per wear, it goes with a bunch of different looks, and is built to last for years to come.

If you’re the kind of guy who thinks $15 jeans have to feel like cardboard and fit like a punishment, let me introduce you to the Amazon special that exceeds my expectations.These budget jeans clock in at just $15, but they don’t feel like a throwaway buy. The denim is a cotton-elastane blend, so while it’s not that stiff, 100% raw denim people love, it looks like classic denim and feels way more forgiving. That hint of stretch allows me to sit, squat, and climb stairs without any restriction. Honestly, the pair is also comfortable enough to travel in, which is not something I say lightly about most cheap jeans.

The fabric has a decent weight to it, too. It’s not paper-thin, not overly rigid; just that sweet middle ground that feels broken-in without looking flimsy. Now, are the jeans perfect? No. The zipper jammed on me a couple of times during the first few wears. Not a dealbreaker, because it loosened up and zipped smoothly after a bit, but worth noting. They’re functional, but they don’t have that tank-like durability you’d expect from a $200 pair.

Uniqlo’s straight jeans from its JW Anderson collaboration are a really clean, easy take on everyday denim. It’s got that classic straight-leg silhouette that’s not too baggy or too slim, so it feels wearable right away. I don’t feel like I’m fighting the jeans, but I also don’t feel swallowed by them. One of the standout qualities is the pre-washed finish. You get a subtle, broken-in fade straight out of the box that doesn’t feel stiff or raw.

Another thing to note: the inseam is 32, and on me this pair runs a little long, so there’s some stacking at the ankle. I’ve found it looks better cuffed. For taller guys, it creates a nice break over the shoe. When it comes time to style, it pairs nicely with oversized tees, structured outerwear, and pretty much anything you’d wear year-round. This pair just sits well, doesn't feel restrictive, and holds up as a reliable “grab-and-go” pair. Plus, it’s more affordable than most options on the list, meaning you can stock up on the three colorways without blowing too much money.

When you’re spending good money on denim, it should be built to last and AGOLDE’s jeans fit the bill. The moment I pulled one leg through, I could tell it was rigid yet surprisingly smooth. It’s made from non-stretch sustainable cotton, which breathes well and softens over time without losing structure. It also has some heft, so I wouldn’t wear it in high-80- or 90-degree temps, but I’ll be reaching for it from fall straight through spring.

Style-wise, it’s a nice departure from your classic blue denim, with a washed-out grey hue that looks sharp with a plain tee or lightweight flannel and boots. My only gripe is the fit: the jeans are already baggy and only come in a 32-inch inseam, which creates more stacking than I’d like at 5 '8". I had mine hemmed slightly to clean up the break. If you’re 5 ‘11” or taller, though, it’ll drape over your shoes or boots the way it’s intended without looking overly bunched.

If you’re looking to lean into the Western workwear trend without going full cowboy, AG’s classic bootcut Jean is an easy place to start. I wore this pair to the Beyonce Cowboy Carter concert to coincide with the album’s theme, but it also works just as well for everyday wear when you want to keep things more understated. For the office, you could wear it with a crisp button-down, simple tee, and minimal sneakers. From a fabric standpoint, the cotton-elastane blend has enough give to move with you, while the premium stretch denim from Japan’s renowned Kaihara mill still feels substantial.

It tapered through the thigh before opening slightly below the knee and sits naturally over cowboy boots. Though it looks just as sharp with clean leather sneakers if boots aren’t your thing. AG only offers one color, but I love the medium-blue wash, which has a clean, lived-in look that adds character without looking overly faded, making it easy to dress up or down. I’d throw it on with a plain white tee and overshirt for the weekend or a denim shirt and leather boots when I want to lean into that classic Americana vibe. Like AGOLDE’s jeans, this pair also only comes in a 32-inch inseam. In this case, it works for guys who are closer to 5’11” or taller.

Wrangler makes one of the most iconic cowboy jeans out there for decades. These were originally made for working cowboys and riders, but this timeless silhouette works for a casual office day or weekend outings. The denim is heavyweight cotton, so right away you feel that structure with a broken-in-over-time feel.

Fit-wise, it sits higher on the waist and runs straight through the leg with room where you actually need it—seat and thigh especially. That’s why guys with thicker legs tend to gravitate toward them. They don’t squeeze you or taper too hard, so you actually get comfort without losing that classic straight-leg Western shape. It’s not chasing trends or trying to be “updated.” And if you’re looking for a more affordable alternative to the AG Jeans, this is your best bet.

Brooks Brothers may be known for Oxford shirts and chinos, but our fashion editors were thoroughly impressed by the Americana brand’s denim. Its slim fit pair is made with premium, mid-weight denim that’s super robust, but soft enough to wear for hours, with a hint of spandex for extra mobility. The fit is where the pair truly shine—a precise, tailored cut that contours through the hips and thighs for a clean silhouette without being super tight. Style-wise, these jeans bridge the gap between smart-casual and laid-back cool, so we’ve worn them to a baseball game as well as an office meeting. These jeans are a dream for a lean to moderately athletic build, though if you have a muscular lower body, you might want to size up.

I’ve probably tested over 30 pairs of dark wash jeans in the past few years, and they all start to blur together. But I can confirm that this one from Tommy Hilfiger is an exception. The straight cut is what really sold me. Because it’s regular from the hip to the hem, it doesn’t pinch when I sit down. You know that awful feeling when you’re at your desk or on the train and your jeans dig into your hips like a vice grip? None of that here. I wore these straight through a long shoot day and a subway ride home without needing to unbutton them the second I walked in the door.

The fabric blend is another win: it’s mostly cotton with a hit of lyocell. That synthetic blend softens things up in a way pure cotton denim never does. It almost feels broken-in right off the rack but still has the structure of a good pair of jeans. And unlike stretch-heavy blends, it doesn’t bag out or sag. The deep rich indigo wash makes it easy to dress things up with a blazer, but casual enough that I can throw on sneakers and a simple tee without it looking too forced.

Our style editors did some research and it turns out that there is no rule saying you can only wear white denim during the summer. Every guy could use a pair in their wardrobe, and make good use of it all year around. The best option we found is this pair from Ralph Lauren that has a pearly white texture, while providing the rugged comfort of a pair of jeans. It’s a straight fit but not too loose, and there was just a hint of stretch for a little boost in comfort.

If you haven’t worn white denim in the past because you’re just not sure how to style it, the trick is to think of something you already know how to work with and just switch this jean in. If you wear chinos in any shade of khaki or brown, a pair of white jeans will give an edgier look without having to change anything else about the outfit. You get the opposite effect when it comes to bluejeans, where swapping them for white elevates the feel of, what is otherwise, the same outfit.

The fit of a black jean is crucial to pulling off dressed up fit, and that is exactly what Lee did here. For starters, I’m 5’8 and the slim-straight cut elongates my profile, giving a sleek, balanced silhouette. This pair is tailored to hug my frame just right without feeling like I squeezed into skinny jeans. When wearing them out on multiple occasions, I still felt like I had enough room to move, thanks to the comforting stretch fabric.

Adorned with branded hardware and the leather logo patch, the aesthetic feels like a nod to the past, while the modern cut still keeps you looking fresh. In terms of style, this pair is the ultimate wardrobe chameleon, working in both casual and semi-dressy settings. It looked just as great with a simple tee and sneakers at a backyard BBQ, as it did with a sport coat and dress shoes at a theater show.

Indigo is the dye that makes most jeans blue. When a brand uses a really rich indigo, like Mavi did here, you get a beautiful range from deep, dark navy and light sky blue. The lighter fades gradually show up and get more pronounced with each wear in a jean like this.

Mavi nailed the modern athletic fit in this jean, providing plenty of room in the hip and thigh, along with a taper in the lower leg that looks clean and stylish. This fit is assisted by a blend of cotton, tencel, polyester, and elastane that is lightweight and stretchy. It was one of the most comfortable jeans for our testers with big quads.

The right fit is the foundation of great jeans. A well-fitting pair should flatter your body type, feel comfortable, and align with your personal style. Here's a breakdown of common fits:

A slim fit jean is slightly tapered from the thigh to the ankle for a modern, streamlined silhouette. It's great for lean, athletic, or average builds who want a sleek, put-together look. Not to get them confused with skinny jeans, they're not nearly as tight, but they are more form-fitting than straight-leg jeans. Because slim fit jeans are so sleek, they pair well with everything—tees, button-downs, and even blazers. In terms of footwear, it can be worn with dress shoes or sneakers.

A straight fit has a uniform width from hip to hem, meaning no tapering at the ankle. It works for all body types, and offers a relaxed but structured look. Offering a balanced silhouette that isn't too baggy or too tight, this fit works great for everyday wear, whether you're pairing it with a flannel, sweatshirt, or polo shirt.

A relaxed cut has extra room in the seat, thighs, and leg, so it’s the most comfortable fit, but it also gives laid-back that’s come back in style. It's ideal for bigger guys, muscular legs, and more breathability. We found it looks great with oversized or relaxed tops to maintain proportion.

A tapered cut is slightly wider in the thighs and gradually narrow toward the ankle. It's a sweet spot between straight-leg and slim-fit jeans—giving you some comfort up top while keeping things clean and tailored below. Ideal for guys with athletic thighs or anyone who wants a streamlined look without going full-blown skinny.

Elastane and spandex (same thing, just different names) are synthetic fibers known for thor serious stretch and bounce-back ability. They’re the secret sauce in modern jeans that makes them way comfier than the stiff, unyielding denim of decades past. A bit of elastane—usually around 1-2%— gives jeans just enough flex to move with you, making them ideal for guys who plan to wear their jeans all day everyday, whether that’s sitting at a desk, running errands, or just kicking back. The trade-off? Stretchy jeans don’t always hold their shape as well as OG 100% cotton denim.

No stretch, no shortcuts. At first, these jeans are stiff. But over time, they mold to your body, creating a custom fit. If you love the idea of breaking in a pair like a well-worn leather jacket, go for this kind—but be ready for a couple uncomfortable weeks.

The holy grail for denim lovers. Selvedge denim is considered top-tier because of its durability, excellent craftsmanship, and the way it develops over time. It’s woven on old-school shuttle looms, which produces a fancy self-finished edge inside the cuff. This means the fabric is denser, less prone to fraying, and typically of higher-quality than mass-produced denim. The real magic? It molds to your body and fades in a way that’s totally unique to how you wear them—no fake distressing needed. The downside? It’s usually stiff at first. Since most selvedge denim is raw (aka unwashed), it starts out rigid, like a thick cotton canvas—but, in the end, it rewards you with some of the best-looking, long-lasting jeans out there.

Your inseam isn't just a number—it dictates whether your jeans stack, skim, or flood. If your denim is too short—you're in capri territory, unless you're purposely rocking cropped jeans. If they're too long, we hope you like puddles of denim at your ankles. For that just-right length, your jeans should either break (gently touch the top of your shoes) or stack naturally if that's your thing.

Most brands offer 30", 32", and 34" inseams, but if you're a shorter or taller guy, look for brands that offer extended sizing or hemming services (Uniqlo and Levi's are great for this). Pro tip: If you like cuffing, go a little longer. If you want a clean, straight-down look, hem them or buy your exact length.

When it comes to denim type in terms of wash and color, you’re choosing between raw vs. washed and light vs. dark vs. everything in between. The right pick depends on how much patience you have, how polished you want to look, and whether you mind a little indigo rub-off. Here’s the breakdown:

This is denim in its purest form: untouched, unwashed, and dark as midnight. It starts out stiff and gradually fades in all the right places based on how you wear them. The trade-off? It takes commitment—you’ll need to break them in, and they might stain your lighter clothes and furniture (hello, indigo bleed).

Pre-washed for softness and color variation, so you get that broken-in look without the break-in period. If you want instant comfort and zero dye transfer, this is your move. If personal fades is your jam, go raw. As for a consistent color and softness from day one, go washed.

The most versatile option—dress it up with a blazer or down with a hoodie. Darker washes are slimming and work in almost any setting. Raw or rinse denim will develop natural fades over time, adding character.

A casual, everyday wash that looks good with everything. Already has some fading, so there’s no awkward stiff phase. Think of it as the sweet spot between too dressy and too relaxed.

Laid-back, retro, and effortlessly cool—perfect for summer or a more relaxed vibe. Looks great with white tees, sneakers, and vintage-inspired fits. Not as dressy as dark denim, but adds character to your wardrobe.

Since 2021, myself and the Men's Health style team have gone full denim detective mode—testing more than 50 different pairs, each worn for at least two weeks at a time, and six hours a day. As someone who’s 5"8" and typically wears 28W/30L, I know what works and what doesn’t. I threw these jeans into every case scenario—casual brunches, city commutes, long-haul flights, running errands, and yes, even squatting for good measure. I took detailed notes on fit, comfort, wash, inseam, and performance (stretch, moisture-wicking, breathability).We checked if they were true to size, how the fabric held up through hours of movement, whether they needed a marathon break-in, and if they could work in a variety of settings. Our testers also include a diverse range of body types to help us ensure an unbiased result for selecting the best jeans for men. We made sure our picks weren’t trendy jeans, but true workhorses that will look great years from now.

As the most versatile article of clothing a man can own, jeans have the ability to traverse many different types of formality. Given that denim originates from workwear, it inherently embodies a casual nature. That's why I suggest throwing in some contrast, like rocking penny loafers with laid-back tailoring.

For a more laid-back look, pair your jeans with a well-fitted tee and canvas or leather sneakers. But when aiming for a smarter appearance, combining dark wash jeans with a crisp button-down shirt or sweater with a pair of boots is a great idea as well.

On the other hand, for a business casual look, throw on a pair of suede loafers with dark denim, an oxford button down, and timeless accessories. Take those same jeans and style your denim with a pair of low-top sneakers like common projects white sneakers, or a heavyweight crewneck sweatshirt and you've got a great weekend look for fall.

100% cotton denim will feel sturdier and often lasts longer—but it can be stiff at first. A cotton-elastane blend adds comfort and mobility. Neither is “better” universally; it depends on how you wear your jeans. If you’re commuting, traveling, or sitting all day, stretch will keep you comfortable. If you want that old-school fade-and-mold-to-your-body experience, go full cotton.

Look at the stitching. Tight, even seams with no loose threads means you have a pair of durable jeans. Check the rivets (those little metal reinforcements at pocket corners), the zipper glide, and the heft of the waist button. Quality jeans often have reinforced belt loops and sturdy pocket bags that don’t feel like tissue paper.

Think about silhouette. The rise—whether high, mid, or low—changes where the jeans sit on your torso and can subtly shift proportions. From there, it’s about the leg shape. Straight-leg jeans are timeless and work on nearly everyone. Tapered cuts offer more room in the thigh with a slimmer opening at the ankle, ideal if you lift or prefer a cleaner line. Slim fits narrow throughout for a sharper look, while flares and bootcuts widen at the hem and are designed to sit neatly over boots (and yes, they’re creeping back into the mainstream). The right combination of rise and fit can make an affordable pair look elevated—or make an expensive pair look completely wrong.

#4839. Kia just made history at Germany’s most prestigious auto awards

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

The judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the new Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.
