#4720. Women Aging Well: Lessons From Memories and Reflections

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

In Tennessee, I walked a magnificent labyrinth inspired by a clock, formed with 1,000 feet of stone, designed as a space of reflection and connection. The artist, Thea Alvin, titled her installation "Time for Love." Since I’ve been thinking about the importance of time as we age, I wandered slowly and quietly on the spiral path toward its center, open to whatever thoughts and feelings emerged. Immediately I relaxed, knowing I would arrive at the center, stay a while, and return along the same path.

As I get older, I am more aware that the path in is never the same as the path out. No path is ever the same because of changes in weather, light, time of day, and the path itself. I am not the same. Just as we can never step in the same river twice, we can never walk along the same path because neither we nor the path remain the same. We evolve over time; as we age, we are continuously unfolding and hopefully, moving toward self-discovery and a center of calm.

I experienced entering the labyrinth as an opportunity to be open and curious about my life at this moment. I have always been drawn to spiral shapes as they are often associated with evolution and transformation. As a nature lover, I notice spiral shapes of pinecones, sunflowers, and other life forms. As I walked the spiral path, I heard the wind, the birdsongs, and the crunching gravel underneath my feet. I listened deeply to myself, without judgment or criticism. When a thought or feeling surfaced, I attempted to observe it and see what it meant. I stayed with that thought and waited to see what else emerged. These were my mind’s musings as I walked to the center. Cultivating curiosity and willingness to stay with a thought or feeling as we age can help us deepen awareness about ourselves, our relationships, and hopefully, encourage us to examine the choices we make in our daily lives.

At the center, I sat on a boulder under a Beech tree, contemplating "Time For Love." The structure was commissioned as a space for family members to come, sit, and remember their loved one who died. The place feels sacred. In my reflection, I recalled people and pets I’ve loved over the course of my life. I felt the warmth of those memories. I realized how much I enjoy reminiscing in this way; quietly, in nature, experiencing sadness and joy. As Thea Alvin intended, I was allocating "Time for Love." Noticing an internal shift, I recognized the necessity of giving myself this time for reflection on love. I needed to do this, and asked myself: How do I use my time compared to how I want to spend it?

Those questions stayed with me as I walked out of the labyrinth. I realized that this thought was not just inspired by the labyrinth but also by Varun Soni, Dean of Religious Life at USC, who spoke at a conference I attended about children and spirituality. He asked: “What deserves more of our attention?” “What would we like to make room for?” “What small change regarding our time could we make today?”

These are important questions to consider at any age; particularly when we are in our older years, when we are more aware of the time that has passed in relation to the time we may have ahead. The final question Dean Soni asked was “What can we do to change what we discover?” Sitting on a rock, under a tree, in the center of "Time for Love," I realized that I can dedicate time to feel the love that I had in my life, and to actively cultivate the love that I feel now. How will I make more time for love? I will remember those I loved; engage in activities I love, be with people I love, share love in ways that make others feel loved, and engage in acts of loving kindness.

As I returned along the spiral path, I felt different. I was different. I discovered that actively engaging with love deserves more of my time and attention. And in making this change, I will feel this connection to love as a vital, positive force in my own aging.

Teichman, S., Pearson, R., Cook, W. A., & Banerjee, A. (2026). Contemplative Training for Mindful Aging: Insights from a Study of Participants' Experiences in a Mind-Body Training Course. Canadian Journal on Aging, 45(2), 263–272.

#4719. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

#4717. The Latest Enamel Pieces by Tiffany & Co. Channel Jean Schlumberger’s Dazzling 1960s Icons

Jean Schlumberger didn’t have a background as a gemologist. The Tiffany & Co. designer got his start in the 1930s with costume jewelry, crafting clips, buttons, and other accessories for Elsa Schiaparelli’s couture collections. “The way he came to jewelry was unpretentious: simple coats of paint on metallic works that looked shiny and lacquered,” says Sylvain Cordier, the Paul Mellon curator and head of the department of European art at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts. “I’mconvinced that starting with costume jewelry very much informed a taste for bold colors.”

A 1960s Jean Schlumberger drawing of a Paillonné enamel bangle for Tiffany & Co.

In the ’60s, at Tiffany, Schlumberger would return to this vivid style in more sophisticated form through the art of paillonné, a process that layers translucent colored enamel on delicate gold or silver leaf, requiring a series of kiln firings. His first paillonné piece, the Croisillon bracelet, debuted in 1962. Philanthropist and Schlumberger devotee Bunny Mellon soon introduced her friend Jackie Kennedy to the style, which the first lady wore so often it became known as the “Jackie bangle.” Schlumberger also applied the enameling to earrings and decorative objects prized by collectors like Mellon, whose Schlumberger collection is held at the Virginia MFA.

Rings from the Enamel by Tiffany collection

Tiffany, which recently announced a collaboration with the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris to preserve Schlumberger’s archives, continues to honor the artistry of his paillonné pieces with its Enamel by Tiffany collection. The house, which employs some of the only remaining artisans skilled in the technique, is expanding these offerings this fall with new pieces that include rings and watches. Despite the decades that have passed since the Croisillon’s debut, Cordier still finds it to be fresh. “When you look at the Schlumberger pieces, there’s this sort of abstract effect,” he says. “I think it’s very modern.”

#4716. You Can See Everything You Ever Want to See in a Movie in You Can See Everything

Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary is three hours long. You’ll wish it went on for three more.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

NATHAN FIELDER HAS become one of the greatest arbiters of what is—or isn’t—the truth. Fielder, whose mainstream career unofficially kicked off with his show Nathan for You, a dry, quasi-documentary, quasi-scripted, quasi-spoof of shows like Undercover Boss, has found a way to level up with each project he’s made over the course of his still relatively short career, each step of the way inviting audiences to not only question the reality of what he’s bringing to the screen, but their own stances and ways of thinking about things broadly.

The road for Fielder has included HBO’s The Rehearsal (another often surreal, often Lynchian project that presents as real, but on a subtextual level asks viewers to question whether any of what he’s depicting was really happening as it was shown) and The Curse, a Showtime/Paramount+ series that he starred in and co-created alongside Emma Stone and Benny Safdie. That show was, surprise, surprise, incredibly thoughtful, layered, and, ultimately, surreal when it comes to its underlying themes of sincerity and intention.

In a way, all of this has led Fielder to his latest project, the new A24 documentary You Can See Everything. The subject is a fitting one for Fielder: Elizabeth Holmes, the former Theranos CEO and convicted fraudster who was the subject of books (Bad Blood) and television shows (The Dropout) about her misdeeds. It makes total sense that someone famous for skirting the truth would be of interest for Fielder, a creator who has now spent so much time examining not only the truth, but what audiences might accept as the truth even given some reason not to.

In 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison. That’s where You Can See Everything comes in: Holmes and her partner Billy Evans invited Fielder (and a film crew, led by co-director Lance Oppenheim) to join them in a home they were renting for complete access during the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in Bryan, Texas, in May 2023. And the film begins there.

And, quite frankly, if you’re considering seeing You Can See Everything, it’s best to leave it there. Fielder gets the access he was promised in the movie, but the joy of the film isn’t only in this exclusive vision of such a notable figure, but how an artist with such a relationship to the truth engages with someone who so notably has, seemingly, bent it. We also get to see Holmes and Evans shot as human beings, removed from any of the prior media circuses that have surrounded them. Fielder and Oppenheim put a fair camera to everything and let the camera do what was promised: See everything.

You Can See Everything has been one of the best-reviewed films of the year, and it lives up to the billing. Just when you think you understand what’s happening and what’s going to happen, you’ll be quickly proven wrong. Just when you think you have a handle on who someone is and what they’re all about… you’ll quickly be proven wrong. The movie is three hours long, which, of course, we know, seems daunting. But by the time it ends, you’ll wish it was going on for three hours more.

Below, we answer some of your questions about You Can See Everything—without spoiling any of the movie’s major twists or turns.

You Can See Everything is now available to watch at home. You can purchase it on Apple TV and rent it on Prime Video—and we suggest doing whichever of those you prefer.

You Can See Everything is, in essence, two movies in one. The first half of the movie is what the trailer and promotional materials for the movie billed: Nathan Fielder joins Elizabeth Holmes (and her new husband Billy Evans) in a home they rented for the 34 days before she reported to federal prison in 2023. This proves to be just as compelling as you’d imagine, as Holmes and Evans are both completely idiosyncratic characters. Moments like when Fielder shows Holmes Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First” bit are instant classics.

Eventually Holmes reports to prison in Bryan, Texas, and the movie is not even halfway over. It’s at this point that your eyebrow should raise, and you do the ‘leaning forward in seat’ meme—because this is when You Can See Everything gets truly wild. The timeline jumps forward two hours, and Nathan Fielder gets up to some of his mind-bending, Rehearsal-type business. At this point, we see some people’s true colors, and also meet some other unexpected guests and surprises in the movie. This second part of the movie is what will blow your mind, and leave you thinking long after the credits begin to roll.

You Can See Everything should be an absolute lock for a number of Oscar nominations, including Best Picture. And it should be a strong contender in one of the acting categories for one person whose appearance we will not be spoiling in this story.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim are the co-directors of You Can See Everything, and both have been key figures in American film and television culture for the last decade.

Fielder is a Canadian-born actor and director (and childhood friend of Seth Rogen) who rose to fame as the creator and star of Comedy Central’s Nathan for You. He’s dabbled in acting here and there—including a role as a limo driver in Rogen’s underrated holiday comedy The Night Before and in the sensational limited series The Curse—but his real calling has come in mind-bending documentary/comedy series like The Rehearsal. In season 2 of The Rehearsal, for example, Fielder actually got his pilot’s license while exploring the aviation industry. (And that was filmed between part 1 and part 2 of You Can See Everything, which is just bananas.)

Oppenheim, who is only 30, has also established himself as one of the best documentarians in the business. His movies Some Kind of Heaven and Spermworld along with his HBO series Ren Faire are deeply layered portrayals of very real people in very real situations; he shoots these documentaries in styles completely different from anyone else, though, lighting them like cinematic spectacles rather than what you probably think of as a documentary in your mind. (Some of the cinematography in You Can See Everything is unbelievably beautiful.)

Primetime, A24’s film about Chris Hansen and To Catch a Predator that came out last month and starred Robert Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo, and Merritt Wever, was Oppenheim’s scripted feature debut.

It probably helps to have information on Elizabeth Holmes’s case—which we recommend getting from any number of sources: The Dropout was the name of the Hulu series that starred Amanda Seyfried as Holmes, but it was also a well-researched and reported podcast that served as the show’s basis. There’s also an HBO documentary called The Inventor and a book called Bad Blood. Any of this would make for a good source for the crimes Holmes was accused of committing. The movie also includes a very brief recap of her case in the early going—not exhaustive, but enough to get the idea.

It does also make sense to have an idea of who Fielder is, what he does, and how he engages with his subjects. We recommend HBO’s The Rehearsal for that, but it’s not 100 percent necessary to enjoy and appreciate the film.

That’s the question, isn’t it? You Can See Everything explores the idea of truth, lies, perspective, and even documentary filmmaking itself. If it makes the most sense to you to take all of You Can See Everything at face value, then please go for it. If you feel the need to question everything, well, that’s okay too. That’s what makes Fielder’s work so unique and so immersive—you can think about it about 100 different ways, and no understanding or interpretation is wrong. It’s set up to feel like a kaleidoscope. You can understand something one way, but maybe something pops up, and suddenly you can’t think about it that way anymore. That’s the point—and that’s what you’ll think about long after the credits roll.

#4714. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#4713. A Minimalist House in Italy Makes the Case for Less

The friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in New York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein. Pawson, then an architectural wunderkind from the United Kingdom, and Smith-Petersen, a young Danish-Italian communications manager for the fashion house, found themselves collaborating on the opening of the brand’s first flagship on Madison Avenue.

Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint. His earliest residential works (a Mallorca summer house for collectors, an art dealer’s London apartment) provided a series of simple surfaces, plinths, and frames—for objects, for vistas, and for life. The same was true at the Calvin Klein store, where designer and client amplified each other’s design approaches in a meeting of minimalist minds.

Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.

The living area features a table and chairs by Poul Kjærholm.

Pawson’s recent residence for Smith-Petersen and her husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, an Armani executive, makes another case for life with less. “The imprint came from childhood: the minimalism, the Danish design,” explains Smith-Petersen, who grew up outside Copenhagen. “Poul Kjærholm was our neighbor,” she adds, name-checking the widely influential midcentury modernist. There were also formative summers spent at the pared-back house her father designed on the Turkish peninsula of Çeşme. About the location, she recalls, “People said, ‘You guys are crazy!’ But it was a place close to nature and the sea. And then later it became a destination.”

A single sculptural tree dots the courtyard.

An oak bed with integrated bedside tables anchors the primary bedroom.

Ninety minutes south of Milan, the patchwork hills of the Val Luretta are far less isolated. Its proximity to the city has attracted editors, artists, and other creatives in search of space and quiet. That tranquility drew Smith-Petersen to the area when she was seeking land on which to build a compound with her younger brother, Henrik, for their families. (She and her husband have two adult sons.) Over the years, she and Pawson had maintained a friendship. “So when Henrik and I found the property, I had this crazy idea: Why don’t I ask John?” says Smith-Petersen. “My brother said, ‘Forget it!’ But we went to visit John and his team in London and it kicked off from there.”

The primary bath’s bespoke vanity, topped in a Grassi Pietri surface

Smith-Petersen stands in the living area.

A view across the dining table toward the minimalist hearth

The resulting structure, realized with project architect Giulio Marchesi, is the irst of two planned homes on the site, one for each sibling. Sitting long and low on the land, like an ivory piano key dropped onto the hillside, the single-story house frames expansive views of the Val Luretta. “The area of the countryside is so dramatic,” reflects Pawson, whose first visit to the site was in winter fog. “In the summer, it’s very different—it’s so lush.”

At some 2,500 square feet, the house is spacious but intimate, with Pawson’s trademark spareness and remarkable warmth. He designed it along one axis, a long corridor connecting the foyer to the open-plan kitchen, dining area, and living area, then bedrooms beyond. White-painted plaster walls and floors of pale-gray stone, sourced nearby in Vicenza, radiate calm. As Pawson explains, understanding the way the body and the eye move through a space is paramount—and can take time. “You’ve got to learn the choreography,” he says. Living in and feeling the house is key.

The yearslong friendship Pawson and Smith-Petersen had forged helped him understand how she would use the space. There would be mornings at the Pawson-designed table, afternoons on the terrace or under one of the century-old oaks, and evenings making dinner in a kitchen brimming with Scandinavian tableware. In solitude or surrounded by family, there’s complete peace on offer.

“Most architects—contemporaries, colleagues—always say, ‘Oh, it’s impossible, a private house,’ ” says Pawson. The process can be “very emotional. And that’s what makes it good.” Luckily for Smith-Petersen, the primary feeling the house evokes is serenity. “I didn’t expect to be in such awe,” she says. “I was never a country person. Sometimes, I try to arrive a day before anyone else is here and do a silent retreat,” she adds. “It’s where I feel best now. It’s pure joy.”

#4712. Winter Essentials Worth Giving—and Keeping

Bring warmth and classic style to city days and outdoor adventures with gear from The North Face.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IT’s AN OFT-EXPRESSED sentiment, but it’s true: The holidays turn people’s attention toward friends, family, and community. There’s a beauty in the selfless, caring gifts people give to others. And while all that giving feels great, the holidays are also a good time to treat yourself. Plus, it’s getting colder.

Whether you equate The North Face with everyday city wear or outdoor adventures, it’s a solid, time-tested spot to get a gift for a loved one (or yourself). The brand has jackets and accessories with familiar winter looks, as well as products with less expected silhouettes that still offer protection from the elements in an understated style.

Here’s a look at some of the best cold-weather gear that will have you wrapping up the gift of warmth and durability… even if that gift is for yourself.

This is an easy gifting win because the warm, hooded, insulated jacket is a recognizable The North Face staple, evoking an unpretentious spin on the brand’s iconic Nuptse Jacket.

It’s familiar, but it’s also practical—the kind of gift you feel good about because it’s going to get a ton of use. (And it can withstand the repeated wears.) The attached hood offers protection from biting winds, and the straightforward color options make it easy to pair with a variety of outfits, whether it’s something fun or part of a heavy bundling during the coldest days of winter. This is the perfect type of winter coat: warm but not too puffy.

The Zaneck Jacket is a great alternative to the Aconcagua, stepping away from the outdoorsy look the brand is best known for. It’s still waterproof and insulated, but it has a longer, more modern cut.

The Zaneck comes with a removable faux fur lining for the hood, which, in addition to being warm, means there are a couple of different looks that can be teased out of it. The straight cuffs add to its stylish feel in a way that doesn’t scream “I’m dressed for warmth and not fashion,” even though it’s doing both.

The Lone Peak Triclimate 2 has a lot in common with the Zaneck. From a distance, they cut a similar silhouette. However, the Lone Peak adds a little versatility if you’re looking for a jacket that can handle a variety of climates.

A removable, insulated inner jacket is attached to a removable, insulated top layer, which is fit for rainy conditions or as a spring or fall jacket. The insulated layer converts the whole thing into a winter-ready jacket. It also sports underarm vents capable of releasing heat in the middle of a long hike, ideal for outdoorsy types. The hood is removable and it’s got adjustable cuffs and an adjustable hem, making this a do-it-all jacket.

It might be easy to ignore the Pertex Jacket. It’s a bit unassuming. It doesn’t cut as stylish of a figure as the Zaneck, but it’s endlessly useful. The lightweight Pertex fabric will keep you dry in a downpour, but it also offers warmth without marshmallow-like bulk.

The lightweight aspect makes this the kind of coat you toss in the backseat on the way to a hike, just in case. It’s also great for layering, whether it’s tossed on over a sweater or layered under an overcoat to make a favorite jacket more winter-ready.

This edition of the classic Base Camp Duffel echoes the design details we love in The North Face’s jackets. While it’s got enough style and a heap of color options for daily use, it’s built for adventure.

Made with water- and tear-resistant fabric, it boasts 71 liters of storage space, a roomier option to the similar 31-liter version. Like all of the brand’s products, it’s built as if the designers have been through the rigors of outdoor adventures (and they probably have). It’s got a sweeping D-zip opening, backpack straps, mesh pockets, and compression straps in case you’re curious if you can pack 73 liters worth of gear into the 71-liter space. (You know you’ve tried.)

The North Face has a lot of hats, none more iconic than this. The Salty Lined Beanie has a classic feel, fitting snuggly over the head with rib-knit texture, a cuffed shape, soft fabric, and ample color options to ensure it will match any jacket or accessory. The Salty Lined Beanie encapsulates the entire The North Face vibe in a small way: It’s stylish enough for a subway ride to work and practical enough for an outdoor adventure. Best of all, it’ll keep your ears warm in either instance.

Often, the best glove is the one that disappears into the outfit. It looks seamless, keeping hands warm without drawing too much attention. The Etip Recycled Glove is about functionality first and foremost, but the simple design and understated colors makes it look good with a variety of winter outfits.

While we all like to pretend we aren’t attached to our phones, the Etip makes a great modern gift because its stretchy fleece delivers a snug fit and the palms have touchscreen compatibility. That means you won’t have to take off your gloves to respond to that important text while the snow is falling.

#4711. Watching 'The Wiz' Is Both Tradition and Medicine

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

I don’t know about your family, but every holiday season starting in November and ending January 1st, my family is definitely watching "The Wiz"; it’s a family tradition. In fact, it’s a tradition for many Black families across America. We pile onto sofas, sing, dance, cry, and debate, and it is tradition. But it also is medicine.

"The Wiz" has been healing Black families since 1978. Science is just now catching up to what your grandmother already knew.

When your family settles in for a ritual you have done together before—the same movie, the same couch, the same debates about the same scenes—your nervous system registers something specific: safety. Predictable shared experience signals to the brain that threat is low and belonging is high. Oxytocin, the neurochemical of trust and bonding, is released during group ritual. Cortisol drops. The vagus nerve, the body’s primary regulation highway, begins to settle. This is not metaphor; it is the physiology of communal gathering, and families have been administering it with precision for decades.

When “You Can’t Win” comes on and you sing along, loud and proud and probably off-key, you are activating your vagus nerve directly. Humming, chanting, and singing stimulate the vagal branches in the throat and chest in ways that measurably increase heart rate variability, the primary marker of nervous system regulation. Group singing amplifies this effect. Research shows that people who sing together synchronize their heart rates. Your family is not only performing. They are co-regulating.

Add in the dancing—spontaneous, in your living room, because you cannot help it when “Brand New Day” comes on and you have activated somatic release. Movement is one of the most effective tools we have for discharging stored stress from the body. Bessel van der Kolk spent a career documenting what dancers and African traditional healers demonstrated before the research did: The body holds what the mind cannot process, and movement releases it.

There is always a moment in "The Wiz" when someone in your family loses it completely. The tears, the laughter, every time; this is not weakness. Shared laughter measurably reduces cortisol, increases natural killer cell activity, and produces documented improvements in immune function. Laughter researcher Lee Berk at Loma Linda University has been publishing on this for decades. Your family’s annual hysteria over the crows or flying monkeys is a clinical-grade immune intervention.

When Dorothy finally gets home, when the music swells, and Lena Horne sings “Believe in Yourself,” and everyone starts crying before the scene even finishes because we have seen it 20 times and it still does this to us; what is happening is awe. Psychologist Dacher Keltner at UC Berkeley has documented awe as one of the most powerful mental health interventions identified in contemporary science. Awe reduces self-focused thinking, increases prosocial behavior, and produces measurable reductions in inflammatory markers. And because awe almost always arrives alongside emotional release—the tears, the full-body exhale, the feeling of being cracked open in the best possible way—it also completes what the dancing started. The body finishes processing what it has been carrying. Your tears are data. Your relief is the point.

"The Wiz" is not just a movie. It is a Black retelling of the oldest story we tell: the journey home to self, to community, to wholeness. Dorothy is doing identity reclamation. The Scarecrow is reclaiming his mind. The Lion is reclaiming his courage. The Tin Man is reclaiming his heart. Our ancestors told this story in circles, around fires, through spirituals. "The Wiz" put it on a screen in 1978, in full Black excellence, and handed it to us as a holiday tradition.

When elders and children watch it together, something else happens. Cultural identity, racial socialization, and connection to Black heritage and community are documented protective factors against the mental health effects of racism. Annual Review of Clinical Psychology research confirms that ethnic and racial identity functions as a clinical buffer. Intergenerational storytelling is not nostalgia. It is immunization.

If "The Wiz" is already your tradition, protect it. Deepen it. Tell your children what is actually happening when you all pile onto that couch. If you lost the tradition somewhere along the way, bring it back this holiday season. If you never had it, start it this year.

Watch it alone if you have to. Let Diana Ross, Michael Jackson, Nipsey Russell, Ted Ross, and Lena Horne be your circle. In my work on public health and ancestral healing, and in my book Ancestral Roots, I return again and again to the truth that chosen family is real family. Your nervous system does not distinguish between blood and chosen. It only knows safety, belonging, and joy.

"The Wiz" delivers all three. Every single time.

Berk, L. S., Felten, D. L., Tan, S. A., Bittman, B. B., & Westengard, J. (2001). Modulation of neuroimmune parameters during the eustress of humor-associated mirthful laughter. Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine, 7(2), 62–76. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11253418/

Van der Kolk, B. A. (2014). The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma. Viking.

Keltner, D., & Haidt, J. (2003). Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion. Cognition and Emotion, 17(2), 297–314. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29715721/

Neblett, E. W. Jr. (2023). Racial, ethnic, and cultural resilience factors in African American youth mental health. Annual Review of Clinical Psychology, 19, 19.1–19.19. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-072720-015146

#4709. Bob Hope at Home: 10 Photos of the Comic’s Life Behind the Curtain

Though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA. “Sometimes I do my best to hide it, but I’ve got a real crush on America,” he wrote in his 1990 memoir, Don’t Shoot, It’s Only Me. “Nobody ever had a girl like her. Nobody ever gave me as much affection, as much honor, or as much real estate.”

Born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings. His family had little money and moved often throughout his childhood. After he found success on stage and it came time to raise his own brood, Hope put down roots in California. Across Toluca Lake and Palm Springs, the star’s homes offered a place to escape the limelight, spend time with his wife and four kids, entertain very famous guests, and indulge in his love of golf.

Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.

Hope (bottom right) at the family estate in Cleveland. The comic’s parents William Henry Hope and Avis Townes Hope are on the porch in the background. Hope was 20 years old at the time of the picture.

Hope and his family moved from London to the United States when he was four. In this 1923 photo, he’s pictured with friends and members of the Hope clan at their Cleveland home. Because money was tight, the family took in boarders to supplement Hope’s father’s income, according to the Library of Congress. In his 1954 memoir, Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope recalls his early days in Cleveland. “The first place we lived by ourselves was Standiforth Court,” he wrote. “We were always on the move. We lived at 2029 Euclid. After that we moved behind the Cleveland Express barns…. It was a long walk between the barns and our house. And if we got home after dark, it was scary…. Next we lived at 1925 East 105th, then at 1913, then at 2029—all on Euclid. We didn’t move very far, only to bigger houses which had more room for roomers.”

Hope and his wife Dolores at home in the 1940s.

Hope married Dolores DeFina in 1934, and the couple adopted their first child, a daughter named Linda, in 1939. That same year, the comic bought a five-acre former walnut grove in Los Angeles’s Toluca Lake neighborhood at 10346 Moorpark Street. He transformed the property into a lavish French Revival estate, featuring a 14,876-square-foot main house with eight bedrooms and eight bathrooms; a two-bedroom, two-bathroom guesthouse; a staff residence; and a pool.

Hope and his grandfather catch up over tea.

In this 1943 photo, Hope is pictured at home with his “Grandpop.” As a young boy in London, Hope lived with his family in a house his grandfather had built. “Grandpop had built a row of houses in Eltham. We lived in one of them. They were put together like stone battleships,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. After moving to the United States, his grandfather went on to build churches in Cleveland and Detroit. Hope reunited with him during a return trip to England in 1939—the star’s first visit since moving across the pond as a child. He recalls the occasion in his memoir, writing that “It wasn’t until I went back to England in 1939 that I got to know [Grandpop]. It was the first time I’d been there since I was four. The English papers reported: ‘One-time shoeshine boy and ironmonger’s assistant comes home.’ The English are supposed to be conservative and not given to exaggeration, but they hooked one there. How could I have been a shoeshine boy or ironmonger’s assistant when I was only four when I left there?”

Back in California, Hope and his wife continued to grow their family. They adopted three more children: Anthony, born in 1940, and twins William and Eleanora, born in 1946. In this circa 1940s photo, the family of six is pictured at home. In Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope reflects on the choice to adopt. “No matter how strongly I feel about the word ‘family,’ Dolores feels even more deeply about it,” he writes. “When we found out that she couldn’t bear children, she began to bend my ear about adoption.” They welcomed their children through The Cradle, an adoption agency in Evanston, Illinois. “Of the five thousand, four hundred and nine babies that The Cradle has placed, there are eight Cradle babies out here in Hollywood,” he continues. “The Hopes are proud to be Cradle parents. I wish I could really tell you what The Cradle means to me here in Hollywood, where all day long the talk is box-office and autographs and premieres and who’ll get the Oscar. ‘The town of make-believe,’ they call it, but don’t get the idea everything is make-believe in Hollywood. There's nothing make-believe about our children. They are real.”

Hope enjoys some family time in the living room with Dolores and two of their children.

Hope’s Toluca Lake estate was more than a family retreat; it was also a gathering place for celebrities and politicians, including Bing Crosby and Richard Nixon. When the property went on the market for $27.5 million in 2013, listing agent Jade Mills said, “[Hope’s] daughter, Linda Hope, would often peek down the grand staircase to see who was coming. She once spoke to Lucie Arnaz and Maria Cooper about doing a book about watching celebrities come and go called ‘Seen From the Landing.’”

The home was “always impressively staffed,” Mills continued. “A full-time cook, butler, estate manager, and two housekeepers manned the property on a daily basis, while additional staff was hired for large receptions.”

Hope, Dolores, and their four kids pose at home in 1958.

In this 1958 photo, Hope and the family pose for a photo on the stairs. In Have Tux, Will Travel, the comic gushes about his wife as a mother. “Dolores has a wise and loving touch with our children,” he writes. “I’m lost in admiration of the job she has done with them, and with the job she’s done with keeping me in line. A lot of children whose fathers are in show business grow up too precocious, too wise, too fresh, too unfunny. That’s not true of our four. Dolores sees to that. She also sees to it that they’re having a devout rearing.”

The family is shown here opening Christmas presents in 1964.

Hope was determined to give his children space at home. “When our kids began to grow up, we fixed up a play room for them and gave them rooms of their own,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. “While we were at it, Dolores and I decided to redo the whole house. We tore out one entire downstairs wall and put in glass, so no matter where we are, we can look out at the garden and enjoy the California sun—if it shows up.”

While his home workspace was connected to the residence, it was its own separate world. “My office adjoins my house,” he writes. “It’s a different project, separate and distinct from our house. In fact, it’s on a different property. It was put up (and is owned) by Hope Enterprises. But it’s handy. The people I want to see on business can walk in and out without disturbing anybody…. It’s a nice set-up.”

Hope was an avid golfer in his free time.

Hope was an avid golfer and built a one-hole golf course at his home in Toluca Lake, where he’s pictured here in this 1990-era photo. He once even said that he considered golf to be his real job. “Golf is my profession,” he said, per ESPN. “Entertainment is just a sideline. I tell jokes to pay my greens fees.” The outlet further reported that he played more than 2,000 courses all over the world and golfed with everyone from Crosby to Dwight Eisenhower and Bill Clinton. “I’ve played all over the world, which means there isn’t a country with a course in which I haven’t three-putted,” Hope said.

Hope and Dolores at home in Palm Springs.

While Toluca Lake served as the family’s primary residence, Hope’s most iconic home was arguably his Palm Springs estate, where he and Dolores are pictured here in 1991. Designed by famed architect John Lautner, the 24,000-square-foot estate featured 10 bedrooms, dramatic arches, and a statement curved roof. The futuristic design closely resembled a spaceship. Hope once joked, “Well, at least when they come down from Mars they’ll know where to go.”

The home’s construction, however, was plagued by setbacks. According to the Los Angeles Times, when building began in the early ’70s, the structure caught on fire and burned down. The project was subsequently delayed for five years, during which time the couple’s interior designer, Arthur Elrod, was killed in a car accident. Dolores then took over the design duties. Lautner’s protégé Helena Arahuete recalled Dolores’s vision: “She wanted everything very ornamented, very rich—you know, gold and pink and black and mirrors everywhere.” Inspired by her friends Walter and Leonore Annenberg’s home, which had a pink roof, Dolores requested that their curved roof be covered in pink terra-cotta gunite.

In 1991, at his Palm Springs pad, Hope hosted “Bob Hope’s Yellow Ribbon Party,” a homecoming celebration for U.S. troops. The soiree included celebrity guest appearances by Brooke Shields, Patti LaBelle, Jimmy Stewart, and former President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty.

Hope died at home in Toluca Lake in 2003 at the age of 100. The estate remained in the family until Dolores’s death in 2011, after which it was listed for $50 million. LA businessman Ron Burkle purchased the star’s Palm Springs pad in 2016, and two years later, added Hope’s Toluca Lake residence to his real estate portfolio.

#4708. Want Headphones Built for Real Workouts? These 9 Survived Runs, Jumps, and Gym-Bag Chaos

Headphones that can handle as much as you can.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Listening to a hyped-up playlist can make all the difference in your workout. As a fitness writer and longtime distance runner, I’ve seen firsthand how the right headphones can make or break a workout. And I’ve worked my way through a range of workout headphones before I found the ones I don’t want to be without.

I used to constantly fiddle with headphones that didn’t fit right, which is a real motivational buzzkill, and once spent 10 minutes trying to hunt down an earbud that popped out mid-run. (I never recovered it.) I’ve also discovered that some headphones are better for certain types of workouts over others. Case in point: My go-to headphones for strength training at the noisy gym are different from what I reach for when it comes to HIIT and running.

No matter the style and fit you prefer, elements like sweat resistance, battery life, sound quality, and adjustability are crucial, too. And, while I love a good bargain, I’ve learned that you can’t just grab any random pair of cheap headphones or earbuds and expect them to do the job well. After multiple rounds of testing, these are the best wireless workout headphones to consider.

The Apple AirPods Pro have always been a reliable pair of headphones for me, and the latest third generation is even better. Whether I’m biking or struggling through heavy reps, it delivers a premium experience, including impressive sound and a comfortable fit. And the latest edition further proves their God-tier status: heart rate, step, and calorie tracking.

It has a sensor that deciphers your pulse through your ear canals, which then calculates calories burned based on heart rate. I like to keep tabs on my heart rate during high-intensity cardio, so it’s a great alternative to wearing a fitness tracker. Just make sure the fit is right to get an accurate reading (four silicone ear cup sizes are available).

It also has motion sensors that can track your steps. All data transfers to the Apple Health app, so you need to own an iPhone or iPad. Luckily, I recently converted (sorry, Android).

When I’m grinding hard at the gym, I want to hear nothing around me except my hype house music. The active noise cancellation drowns out any grunters, loud gym music, TVs, and general unnecessary background noise. I feel like it’s just me and my music, so that I can laser-focus on the task at hand.

But when I need to maintain awareness during outdoor runs, I turn on transparency mode to hear oncoming traffic and people nearby. I also like that it automatically lowers my music when it detects me talking to someone. It has an IP57 rating, meaning it’s sweat and dust-resistant, and can be submerged in a meter of water for up to 30 minutes in case of any accidental puddle drops (been there). As someone who sweats a lot, each bud repels moisture very well and doesn’t fall out of my ears when jumping or running. Plus, sweat never clogs my ears—something I experienced with regular AirPods. Battery life could be better for all-day wear, but it’s good for workouts (assuming you’re not working out all day). I hit the gym after work, and the power is always drained after an eight-hour day. On the flip side, it’s easy to juice up in 15 minutes with the charging case (it offers up to 30 hours of battery life per charge). To fully restore the battery, make sure to charge overnight. Read More: Best Fitness Trackers

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones are an absolute treasure. I own a lot of headphones, but the sound quality always keeps me coming back for more. The over-ear design completely covers my ears, providing A-grade noise cancellation at prime-time hours.

The sound is immersive with balanced, deep bass that doesn’t feel piercing—an issue with lower-quality headphones I tested. I blast my tunes at full volume when getting in the zone, and I never feel uncomfortable.

They look bulky, but looks can be deceiving. They never budge, even when speed walking at an incline or doing fast-paced plyometric drills. I’ve worn it during box jumps and ice skaters, and it stayed put.

Just note it’s not water resistant for intense cardio like spinning and running, where you’ll work up a sweat—although the plush padding rimming the headband and ear cups can easily be wiped clean.

Like the Apple AirPods Pro 3, I have to charge it daily in the included case, so make sure to keep the cable on hand for quick power-ups.

Read More: The Best Slim Fitness Trackers

If you really just can’t with the possibility of your earbuds falling out, but still want a compact option, Dr. Dre delivered just what you need: the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2. It has hooks that seamlessly glide over the ears, ensuring a proper fit that stays put. And compared to the previous iteration that launched six years ago, it’s now smaller and lighter, and shares many of the same features as the AirPods Pro 3 (Apple does own Beats, after all), including active noise cancellation, transparency mode, and heart rate monitoring through the Beats app.

I’ve put it to the test during long runs, sprints, low-impact biking, and strength training. The verdict? It performs as sleekly as it looks. The sound is crisp and rich, while the bass is heavy without being overbearing.The sweat resistance is a notch below AirPods with an IPX4 rating, meaning it can withstand light rain but can’t be submerged. I’ve gotten caught in the rain one too many times while wearing these—yet, the sound quality is still the same as it was straight out of the box. And battery life is actually slightly better than AirPods, offering up to 45 hours with the charging case.However, this pair feels more uncomfortable than the Apple AirPods Pro 3. The material feels a little too hard for my liking. If you plan on walking or running for hours, the best overall is the way to go.

The last thing you want is uncomfortable headphones when in the midst of PRing your next barbell squat. Working out is tough enough, so having a pair that’s übersoft will take away some of the pain. Meet the Sony WH-1000XM6—a splurge that’s worth the investment.

Thick foam on the ear cups feels like lying on a pillow, while it also seals sound better for superior noise cancellation. The wide headband is plush and fits securely onto the head without being too tight. MH senior gear and commerce editor Ryan Brower throws it in his gym bag whenever he has strength training on deck. He also appreciates the adjustable smooth slider for a custom fit, calling it a fluid mechanism.

The headphones use 12 microphones to isolate and cancel out sound to deliver an immersive listening experience. Vocals and instruments sound balanced and rich, with Brower calling the sound quality superb. Battery life can run for up to 30 hours, while just three minutes of charging can provide three hours—perfect if you’re in a rush to hit the gym.

Brower’s only gripes are the lack of sweat resistance for high-intensity activities, like running or spinning, and that it feels a little bulky. So, he reserves it for less strenuous pursuits.

If you’re into an over-ear design in headphones, you know they can get hot and sweaty fast. But the Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones feel surprisingly breathable on—for an over-ear headphone. The ear cups are made from a lightweight material that feels breezy against your ears, minimizing extra sweating while you work out.

These headphones also have an impressive battery life of 40 hours, which is only second on our list to the Powerbeats Pro 2. Skullcandy clearly designed these headphones for convenience, with plenty of buttons within easy reach. As a result, you can quickly turn the volume up or down without missing a beat. If active noise cancellation is a must for you, scroll up—while the sound quality on these headphones is excellent, they won’t help you fully tune out the world.

The Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones don’t have an official IPX rating, but they have a special sweat- and water-resistant nano-coating to protect your gear. (The ear cup pads are also removable for easy cleaning.) A big draw of these headphones is the strong bass, which comes in handy during tough workouts. As someone who loses nearly everything, I appreciate the built-in Tile technology to help you find your headphones with the Tile app if you misplace them.

I first tested the Bose Open Ultra Earbuds last fall, and they’ve been my favorite pair for distance running ever since. These earbuds aren’t going anywhere thanks to a design that’s similar to a clip-on earring. Just gently hook these on your ears and move on. The style is perfect for people like me who have been burned in the past by an earbud falling out and vanishing forever.

As an early morning runner who regularly crosses streets, I appreciate the open-ear audio these earbuds deliver. I can hear my music perfectly, but still can detect things like chirping birds to give me a solid awareness of my surroundings. You can adjust the volume, skip songs, and flip between immersive and stereo sound with a tap on your earbuds, making it easy to switch things up mid-run.

A heads up: If you’ve never used an earbud style like this in the past, you may need to give your ears a little time to build up to wearing them. My ears were a little sore when I first started wearing the Open Ultra Earbuds, but I don’t even feel them when they’re on now. These earbuds are also IPX4 rated for water resistance, so they do just fine with light splashes or rain—just make sure you don't wear these to swim laps.

The earbuds have a seven-hour battery life, which is lower than several others on this list. But I’ve never had an issue with them dying on me. I just pop them in their charging case when they’re not in use.

Some people are going to struggle to get earbuds to fit, no matter what they do. If you have smaller ears and you’re over flipping through different ear tips in hopes something will fit, the Beats Powerbeats Fit are a solid choice. These earbuds actually fit inside your ears like a hearing aid with the help of flexible wingtips that really lock them in there.

These earbuds are small, but they deliver the top-tier sound quality you’ve come to expect from Beats. That includes the options to flip between active noise cancellation and transparency modes, so you can use these to tune out loud gym-goers or to be aware of your surroundings during outdoor workouts.

These earbuds pair seamlessly with Apple and Android phones, making them an equal opportunity headphone. They also have an IPX4 rating for sweat and splash resistance, so you can wear them in the rain, but not to swim laps. While the Powerbeats Fit comes with four different tips, your ears will still need a little time to get used to these before wearing them on, say, a 10-miler.

The earbuds do kind of jam in there, and it can take some time to get used to the feel of the wingtips. But if you’re looking for a discreet pair of headphones that aren’t going anywhere, you can stop your search here.

If you want secure earbuds that aren’t an investment, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20 fits the bill. It costs a third of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and shares the same ear-hook design that doesn’t budge when pushing your limits during high-impact workouts. The sound is shockingly premium given the $80 price tag. If I were doing a blind test, I’d think it costs at least $200.

The strong noise cancellation blocks out every peep imaginable at the gym. From loud gym music to weights slamming, I can’t hear a thing except my jams. But when I don’t want to be super locked in, I switch to “normal” mode so I can listen to background noise. This mode is handy when running or walking at night. And when things get too wet during intense grinding sessions, the IP67 sweat-resistance saves me. Although I haven’t tested it while swimming, it can withstand water submersion beyond one meter for about 30 minutes.

The silicone ear hooks are soft, flexible, and extremely comfortable. I find myself reaching for it outside of the gym and often forget it’s even on my ears, which I’m not mad about—it makes a great cool-girl accessory. The only downside of wearing it for too long is that the battery will drain after about eight hours. Luckily, the charging case has two days' worth of battery life—so no excuses to skip a workout.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are my go-to for long-distance running because of the wrap-around and open-ear design that stays in place. It’s no surprise it’s a TikTok-viral favorite among runners and our editors.

The sweat-resistance rating is one notch below our best overall, with an IP55 score, meaning it can withstand intense rain during rough outdoor conditions. Moisture from sweat is never an issue since the design hangs over the ear and doesn’t go in the canal. It even alerts me with a vibrating beep if moisture is present in the port while charging.

If blocking out noise is your priority, you should consider other options, as this pair doesn’t offer noise cancellation. I don’t love that I can’t be fully engaged in my music, but that’s the trade-off for running safely. Unlike other headphones I tested in this guide, the sound emits outside of the eardrum using bone conduction technology, which is when noise is transmitted through vibrations in the skull to reach the ear. I hear every sound, from people talking to traffic, so I give it a perfect score for maintaining awareness. I deem it an essential pair if you train early in the mornings or at night. Just note it’s not going to be the same listening experience as the Apple AirPods Pro 3, for example.

The battery life is nowhere near the capacity of the Apple AirPods Pro 3, with only about 12 hours of playtime, so I find I have to charge it weekly for an hour. The flip side is that it only takes 10 minutes to get two hours of battery life if I quickly need it before a run.

Full disclosure: They come in two sizes, but tend to run large, which is why I went with the mini size. I ordered the standard size first and had to return them (small head probs).

If you plan on running, spinning, or doing other high-intensity training, it’s best to have headphones that can withstand sweat. They should have an IP rating, which is a protection score for how well electronics can resist water. “IPX4 or higher is perfect for working out,” says Joe Smith, an audio specialist at Music Critic. All options on this list have at least an IPX4 rating.

But our best budget option, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20, has an even better score of IP67, meaning it can handle being submerged in just over one meter of water for 30 minutes. If headphones aren’t made to withstand sweat, it’s best to reserve those for lower-intensity workouts.

Having your headphones die during a half-marathon is not the vibe (been there). Using a pair with good battery life is crucial to ensuring the tunes are always going strong during a long workout. With select pairs, it can be dependent on whether or not select features are in use.

For example, the total playtime for the new Apple AirPods Pro 3 from a single charge (with case) is up to 10 hours with active noise cancellation turned off, but only up to eight hours with it turned on. Carl Prouty, a tech expert at Abt, recommends snagging a model that charges fast in case you forget to plug them in the night before.

Noise cancellation is a function that utilizes a microphone hidden inside the earbud or earcup to analyze frequencies that emit opposite sound waves, thus helping to reduce background noise. Blocking out surrounding noise is great for staying focused and immersed, but it’s not the safest feature in desolate areas like quiet trails, busy streets, or at night.

I prefer an open-ear style to maintain awareness during outdoor runs. If you’re not a fan of that design, other options on this list allow you to turn noise cancellation on and off. “If you still want to be able to hear what's going on around you while also listening to music, look for a model with a good ambient and pass-through mode,” says Prouty.

You have a lot to choose from in a workout headphone, and each has its pros and cons. Earbuds rest inside your ears to deliver sound without bulk. These tend to fit comfortably, but may pop out if you don’t get the fit right. Ear hook earbuds add an extra layer—a hook that goes over your ears—to help combat this issue. There are also open-style headphones that hook over your ears and around the back of your head to keep them in place.

A newer category of these is open earbuds that clip over your ear like a clip-on earring, while nestling into your ear like an earbud. Finally, over-ear headphones have soft cups that fit over your ear for a classic look. While these usually do a good job staying in place, they may feel hotter during intense workouts than other designs.

As a distance runner, I rely on good music to keep me hyped up and entertained on long runs. I’ve tested dozens of pairs of wireless headphones for working out over the past decade and learned what features make pairs stand out. Only workout headphones with good sweat resistance, battery life, noise cancellation, and sound transparency made the final cut.

Because everyone has different needs in a workout headphone, I also leaned on experiences from Women’s Health editors, along with Men’s Health senior gear and reviews editor Ryan Brower. Each pair was used in different environments during cardio and strength training sessions to see how they performed when put to the test during workouts. Those included 5- to 10-mile runs, indoor cycling workouts, HIIT sessions, and more general lifting at the gym.

#4706. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with no subscription required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4705. Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade: 5 Facts You May Not Know

Every year, millions of people line the streets of New York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible. In honor of the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, Hoda Kotb, who has hosted the event since 2018, brought AD for a look inside the 72,000-square-foot studio where all of the floats, balloons, and costumes are designed and constructed. Read on to discover the most interesting behind-the-scenes tidbits that we learned.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio

“Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” says executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year. Before the Macy’s team moved into their current space, the magic happened inside a former Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, New Jersey.

Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss

The first parade in 1924 featured animals from the Central Park zoo, including elephants, lions, tigers, and bears. They were soon replaced with the giant character balloons that the parade is famous for today, but even that tradition used to look different. From 1928 to 1932, the balloons were released into the air and people were encouraged to find them for a cash reward. “That went on until things got a bit more challenging in the skies, because private aircraft would actually go and track them and try to grab them and bring them back down to Earth,” explains Coss. “But in 1931, there was a blue hippo that was released, never to be seen again. And this year, the blue hippo is making his triumphant return back to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.”

In addition to the blue hippo, balloons of yore will be making a comeback for the 100th parade, including Felix the Cat, the first character balloon to appear in the parade, and Underdog, who hasn’t made an appearance at the parade in 42 years. Snoopy, the most frequently recurring balloon, will return this year as his alter ego Joe Cool for the first time.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio

“The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been in production since my first day here, five years ago,” says Coss. “This year the stakes are high; you only have one shot at the 100th.” To mark the occasion, there will be seven new balloons, six new floats, and one new “balloonicle,” or balloon vehicle.

Hoda Kotb welcoming AD to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio

From concept drawings to weatherproofing, it can take up to six months to complete a parade float. “While a lot of the work here requires a lot of planning, a lot of design, a lot of engineering, our end goal is to bring people together, to inspire joy, to create that new tradition,” says Coss, “whether it’s a family experiencing it for the first time or experiencing it for the 25th time.”
